title: Microbatching, KV Sharding, and MoE Cost Tradeoffs — Arch Tuning for Llama/Mistral/Qwen
summary: Detailed technical session focused on reducing tail latency and unit cost for high-throughput LLM inference in Peregrine's private VPC. Covered microbatch sizing, KV cache sharding strategies, rope decay/scale implications for Llama/Mistral/Qwen, MoE router throttling and cost modeling, and quantization impacts on accuracy and memory. Agreed on a next-step benchmark matrix and on-prem POC in Peregrine's lab cluster.

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-14 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Avery Lopez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Martin (Redwood SE), Elaine Chen (Peregrine CTO), Marco Reyes (Infra), Nirav Shah (ML Lead), Priya Kapoor (SRE)

Auto-summary: technical deep-dive covering batching, kv cache, rope scaling, MoE costs, quantization and VPC considerations. Action items captured at end.

[00:00:00] Avery: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick run of show — Samir will walk the runtime perf considerations, we'll dig into KV sharding and microbatching, then talk MoE routing costs and rope scaling specifics for your Llama / Mistral / Qwen mix, and finish with on-prem/VPC requirements.
[00:00:18] Elaine: Sounds good. We're mostly worried about tail latency and overall token cost — our product is conversational with very spiky traffic.
[00:00:25] Samir: Right, and that's actually going to drive a lot of the config choices. Two quick clarifiers: what are your typical sequence lengths and the percent of long-turn conversations?
[00:00:32] Nirav: Median seq is about 120 tokens, 90th percentile around 900, but we have a long-tail to 2k+ for context windows on some users.
[00:00:40] Priya: Also important: everything needs to live inside our VPC, we have to integrate with our KMS and audit logs — SOC2 is on the roadmap.
[00:00:48] Jules: Great, thanks. I'll call out design patterns as we go — microbatching windows, prefix caching, KV sharding topology, and then MoE-specific things like router overload and expert capacity.

--- Microbatching and latency tradeoffs ---
[00:01:12] Samir: Microbatching increases throughput but adds queueing latency. Our runtime defaults to a ~4–8ms window at X requests per worker, but for your tail we should consider an adaptive window that collapses when queue depth is low. For example, at median seq 120, microbatch size 8 with continuous batching gives good GPU utilization. But at 900–2k, the per-token compute dominates and you want smaller microbatches to avoid multiplying tail latency.
[00:02:05] Marco: Can you quantify the tradeoff? We need ballpark dollars per million tokens with different batchings.
[00:02:12] Samir: Sure — rough numbers off our baseline runtime: with a Mistral-like 34B quantized to int8 and microbatch 8 you can get ~2.3M tokens/hour per A100-equivalent. Shrink microbatch to 2 you drop throughput ~30–40% but tail P99 improves by 25–40ms depending on seq. Cost per million tokens moves accordingly — we'll put precise rates into the spreadsheet.
[00:03:01] Elaine: How about streaming & partial responses? Our front-end shows token streaming and we can't have big front-end stalls.
[00:03:08] Samir: Streaming interacts with batching — smaller microbatches mean earlier first token latency. Redwood supports head-of-line priority for streaming requests so they can bypass batching windows in latency-sensitive modes.

--- KV cache sharding/topology ---
[00:04:05] Samir: KV cache is the big lever for long context. Options: per-GPU local KV (fastest but replication heavy), sharded KV across GPUs with a router (good memory efficiency but network overhead), or hybrid where recent prefixes are local and long-tail caches live on a remote fast KV store. For your 2k contexts, per-GPU local KV becomes memory taxing quickly — with Llama-2 style attention keys and 2k seq, one shard can burn through GPU memory.
[00:05:00] Nirav: What about KV sharding for Qwen — any gotchas?
[00:05:05] Jules: Qwen uses slightly denser KV due to its rotary encodings; rope scaling can interact here. We recommend a 16-way sharded KV for 2k seq on 80GB GPUs to keep per-device memory under control. That does introduce a cross-GPU allgather every token for certain operations unless you use pipeline parallelism tuned for KV locality.
[00:06:02] Marco: Network overhead concerns — we're on a 100Gb fabric in our lab, but if we go on-prem with smaller racks we may be 25Gb.
[00:06:11] Samir: 100Gb is fine for sharded KV at moderate QPS. At 25Gb you need to either increase local KV fraction or accept higher tail latency. Another option is to co-locate experts/routers with KV shards to reduce cross-host traffic — essentially affinity scheduling.

--- ROPe scaling and positional encodings ---
[00:08:00] Samir: Rope scaling is subtle: scaling RoPE/rotary values when you up the context window can give you longer extrapolation but you can also destabilize probability mass for older tokens if you scale too aggressively. For Llama, we tend to use linear rope decay with a small alpha to maintain stability; Mistral has been more robust to mild rescaling. Qwen is model-dependent — we'll check the vendor notes but expect you may need to retune the decay factor when moving to 2k/4k windows.
[00:09:02] Nirav: Any impact on KV cache invalidation?
[00:09:06] Jules: If you change rope parameters you must recompute KV encodings or you get mismatch. That means model variant pinned per deployment — rolling the model with new rope scaling is a heavy op. Prefer runtime-level techniques first (cache eviction policies) until you commit to retraining or fine-tuning with different rope.

--- MoE routing costs & throttling ---
[00:11:20] Samir: For MoE models the router is the cost control point. Two big things: expert fanout (k) and expert capacity. Higher k increases quality slightly but multiplies dispatch overhead. Also token copying to multiple experts increases memory and compute at routing time. Our recommendation for cost-sensitive workloads is k=1–2 with capacity-fold of 1.25–1.5. For bursty traffic you may see router overload where queued tokens wait for expert slots; we implement overflow queues and graceful degrade to dense model variants.
[00:12:02] Marco: So what's the price delta vs dense models?
[00:12:08] Samir: It depends — with a 64-expert MoE and well-packed traffic you can save 2–3x in FLOPs for the expert layers vs a dense 70B, but routing and memory overhead plus peak expert loss can reduce those gains. Our cost model in the sheet simulates realistic burst patterns and shows effective savings of 1.4–2x in most enterprise scenarios, less if your traffic is highly spiky or you need k=4.
[00:12:55] Elaine: Is it safe to mix MoE and dense in different routes?
[00:13:01] Jules: Absolutely — Redwood supports route-based model selection. For short context, low-latency routes use dense quantized models; for long-context batch jobs you can route to MoE variants. Also automatic fallback if router is overloaded.

--- Quantization: int8 / int4 / hybrid ---
[00:14:30] Samir: Quantization is a spectrum: int8 usually gives near-native quality for most models with big memory wins, int4 needs careful per-layer calibration and can drop accuracy on instruction-heavy tasks. Hybrid quantization (int8 for attention/FFN critical kernels, int4 elsewhere) is a strong sweet spot. For Mistral we've seen ~6–8% memory drop with int8 and ~12–18% with mixed int4 but quality hits vary by prompt. We recommend running your eval prompts through quantized candidates before rolling.
[00:15:20] Priya: Does Redwood do GPU kernel selection automatically? We use some NVIDIA optims and also some open kernels in our stack.
[00:15:28] Samir: Yes — runtime picks kernels by model, sequence length and hw. For int8 we default to optimized cuBLAS/cuDNN paths where available, fall back to custom kernels for int4. There's a perf delta; we'll list per-model kernel recommendations.

--- VPC / on-prem specifics ---
[00:16:40] Avery: Quick ops note — Peregrine needs Private deployment with customer-managed control plane and KMS/HSM for keying. Also audit logs for inference events (token-level logs optional). What restrictions do you have on telemetry?
[00:16:55] Elaine: We can share anonymized telemetry; raw prompts must not leave the VPC.
[00:17:02] Jules: That's compatible — Redwood Private can run the serving plane inside your VPC and route metrics to a separate observability endpoint that you control, or ship only aggregated stats. For SOC2 readiness we support SAML SSO, RBAC, and KMS integrations with Azure/AWS/GCP KMS or customer-managed HSMs.

--- Deep dive: example perf configs ---
[00:18:50] Samir: Example config A (low-latency): dense Mistral-34B int8, microbatch 2, priority for streaming, local KV fraction 0.6, no MoE. Expected P50 first-token ~40ms on A100-type, P99 ~220ms depending on network.
[00:19:20] Samir: Example config B (cost-efficient long-context): MoE-64 expert variant, k=1, microbatch 8, sharded KV (16-way), hybrid quantization int8+int4, affinity scheduling, expected throughput gains 1.6–1.9x but P99 higher under spikes.
[00:19:45] Nirav: How do we measure QoE when we try quantized MoE? Any recommended evals?
[00:19:52] Jules: Use held-out prompt sets across your top 50 failure cases, measure semantic similarity, hallucination rate, and a small human rating panel for edge cases. Redwood Optimize can automate some of this and generate regression alerts.

--- Adversarial and edge cases ---
[00:21:30] Samir: A few pitfalls we've seen: 1) Changing rope without KV recompute, 2) mixing quantized and non-quantized keys accidentally, 3) router spill to main thread causing GC with python runtimes. Avoid mixed encodings in a single route and pin model versions for long tests.
[00:22:05] Marco: You mentioned affinity scheduling — does Redwood surface that in the control plane?
[00:22:10] Jules: Yes, in the Console you can annotate workloads with placement hints and set autoscaler policies by route. Those are enforced by the orchestrator.

--- Live Q&A and clarifications ---
[00:24:00] Elaine: If we want to try a small on-prem pilot, what are the minimum rack requirements?
[00:24:07] Samir: For a representative pilot with 2k seq and sharded KV you want at least 4x80GB GPUs on 100Gb with a head-node for routing and one fast NVMe for remote prefix store. If you only have 25Gb, scale down sharding and accept higher tail.
[00:24:35] Nirav: For the POC, can we start with 2x A100 80GB and scale?
[00:24:40] Jules: Yes for a tiny POC but expect limited sharding and you'll be CPU-bound on routing if QPS hits. We recommend starting with 4 GPUs for realistic MoE routing tests.

[00:26:00] Marco: On the security side, how do we audit token access? We need to show who requested what in a way that doesn't expose content.
[00:26:10] Avery: We support hashed token-level audit trails where we log metadata and a hash of the prompt. Full content can be stored only inside your KMS-protected store if you choose.

--- Benchmarks & metrics to capture ---
[00:27:00] Samir: For benchmarking capture: per-token throughput, first-token latency, tail percentiles (P90/95/99), memory footprint per device, KV hit rate, router queue length, expert utilization, and algorithmic ops for MoE layers. Also run synthetic burst tests to emulate your peak zones and a real traffic replay.

--- Example exchange about unexpected transcription artifacts (meta) ---
[00:30:10] Speaker 2: (inaudible)
[00:30:14] Samir: Sorry, could you repeat?
[00:30:16] Marco: I said we'll share the traffic shape — 95th percentile burst is 120 requests/sec for a 30s window, then cooldown.

--- Wrap-up and next steps ---
[00:58:00] Avery: Recap: Redwood will share the perf spreadsheet, microbatch scripts and initial benchmark plan. Peregrine will provision VPC test access and share prompt/traffic samples. Plan for on-prem POC week of 2026-05-25.
[00:58:30] Elaine: That's great — appreciate the thoroughness.
[00:58:40] Nirav: One more ask — can you include an example of the fallback policy when a router gets overloaded? We need docs for our SRE playbook.
[00:58:52] Samir: Yep — we'll include the fallback flow: degrade to dense route, increase retry backoff, and throttle non-priority requests.
[00:59:10] Jules: I'll put links to the console screens and the affinity policy docs in the follow-up email.
[01:00:00] Avery: Thanks all — end call.
